title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
Double Take: guess first
Before you scroll: a driver starts on pole. Where do they usually finish?
And if you scored how closely the finishing order follows the starting order, from 0 (no link at all) to 1 (identical every time), what score would you give it?
Write your guess down, then open the box.






TipTake a second look





Of the 85 drivers who started on pole and finished the race, 60% won, and 75% finished first or second.
And how closely does the finishing order follow the starting order overall? On a scale from 0 (no link) to 1 (everyone finishes exactly where they started), it scores 0.73: a strong link, but far from a certainty. I guessed 0.37.

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
The picture








Figure 1: Each dot is the typical (median) finish for drivers starting in that grid slot; the bar shows where the middle half of them finished.





Take a second look: Look at the right-hand side of the chart: drivers who start 15th or further back usually finish a few places higher than they started. Part of that gain is free: when cars ahead retire, everyone behind them moves up a place.
Some of it is also fast cars that started out of place, after a grid penalty or a bad qualifying, working their way back to where they belong.

-- f1_grid_vs_finish: this table is used/read by Exhibit 1
-- one row per classified finisher who started from the grid, 2022-2025
--
-- Config notes (kept out here because SQL comments can't go inside the braces):
--   materialized: on DuckDB, write a Parquet file that R and Power BI read directly;
--                 on Fabric/Snowflake (February), build an ordinary table. No forked SQL.
--   location:     relative to where dbt runs (the dbt\ folder), like the profile's db path.

{{ config(
    materialized = ('external' if target.type =='duckdb' else 'table'),
    location = '../data/processed/f1_grid_vs_finish.parquet'
) }}

WITH finishers AS (

    SELECT
        result_id,     -- carrying through so the mart has a unique key to test
        season,
        round,
        driver_code,
        team,
        grid,
        finish_position
      FROM {{ ref('stg_f1__results')}}    -- ref() is what draws the lineage arrow
     WHERE grid > 0                       -- pit-lane starts have no grid slot to compare - removing
       AND finish_position IS NOT NULL    -- only classified finishers; this is exhibit logic
)

SELECT
    result_id,
    season,
    round,
    driver_code,
    team,
    grid,
    finish_position,
    -- positive = progressed forward, negative = lost places
    grid - finish_position AS places_gained,
    -- average gain per team in the season, repeated on all rows for that team and season
    avg(grid - finish_position) OVER (PARTITION BY season, team) AS team_avg_gained
  FROM finishers  

  -- Test: uv run dbt show --inline "select count(*) as all_rows, count(*) filter (where grid = 0) as pit_lane, count(*) filter (where finish_position is null) as not_classified from {{ ref('stg_f1__results') }}"
What to notice: the two where filters (pit-lane starts and non-finishers leave here, and the page says so below); the window function, which gives every driver their team’s average without collapsing rows; and the config block, which writes Parquet on DuckDB and a table on any other warehouse.


"""Pull F1 race results from the Jolpica API (via FastF1) into data/raw/f1/.

Run from the repo root:  uv run python python/f1_ingest.py
Data licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (Jolpica). See data/DATA_SOURCES.md.
"""

from pathlib import Path
import time 

import fastf1 
import pandas as pd
from fastf1.ergast import Ergast

# Settings defined here, at the top, so everything below can use them
SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
CACHE_DIR = Path("data/raw/fastf1_cache")
OUT_FILE = Path("data/raw/f1/race_results.parquet")

def main() -> None:
    CACHE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    OUT_FILE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    fastf1.Cache.configure(cache_dir=str(CACHE_DIR))

    ergast = Ergast(result_type="pandas", auto_cast=True)
    frames = []                                                       # One table per race
    
    # For each season, fetch results
    for season in SEASONS:
        schedule = ergast.get_race_schedule(season=season)

        for rnd in schedule["round"]:
            resp = ergast.get_race_results(season=season, round=int(rnd))
            time.sleep(1)

            if len(resp.content) == 0:                          # a cancelled race has no results: skip it
                print(f"{season} round {rnd}: no results, skipped")
                continue

            race = pd.DataFrame(resp.content[0])                # results table
What to notice: results are cached and requests are throttled to one a second, so the API is never hammered and a re-run resumes instead of starting again.

# ---- 2. Spearman's rank correlation ---------------------------------------------------------
# Spearman's rank correlation: measures how closely starting grid position
# and finishing position agree in rank order (-1 to +1). A value near +1
# means drivers tend to finish roughly where they start; near 0 means grid

  method = "spearman",
  exact = FALSE          # positions repeat across races (lots of ties), so use the approximation
)

# rho: Rank correlation coefficient (-1 to 1) measuring how closely two rankings align

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
In plain English
Drivers who start near the front usually finish near the front. But fast cars qualify well and race well, so a lot of what looks like the power of pole position is really the power of the car.

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
The technique
Spearman’s rank correlation (family: association), then linear regression with a covariate (family: modelling).
Grid and finishing positions are both ordinal: the order matters, but the gap between 1st and 2nd isn’t necessarily the same as between 15th and 16th. Spearman works on ranks, so it doesn’t assume equal gaps. The regression then asks how much finishing position changes per grid place, first on its own and then comparing drivers in the same car (each team in each season counts as one car).
Assumptions and checks








Assumption
How I checked
Result




Results are independent
Drivers in the same race are linked (only one can finish 1st)
The interval for the correlation resamples whole races. The regression’s intervals will be too narrow, so treat them as rough


The relationship is roughly a straight line
Residuals-vs-fitted plot
The average miss stays near zero across the range: a straight line is a fair summary


Positions run from 1 to 20
By design
Front-runners can finish far worse than predicted but not much better; noted as a limitation


Only classified finishers are included
15 pit-lane starts and 216 non-classified results were dropped
Survivorship risk: see the caveats

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
What the numbers say

Across 1,609 classified finishes in 92 races (2022–2025), the rank correlation between grid and finish is 0.73 (95% interval 0.69 to 0.77, resampling whole races). That’s a strong link.
Ignoring the car, each place further back on the grid goes with finishing about 0.65 places further back (95% CI 0.62 to 0.68). Grid alone explains 52% of the variation in finishing position.
Comparing drivers in the same car, that falls to about 0.42 places (95% CI 0.38 to 0.45): 36% smaller. Knowing the car raises the share explained to 64%.

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
The brain trap: narrative fallacy
We like tidy stories: “he won because he started on pole”. The start is visible and memorable; the car’s pace across the whole weekend isn’t, so the story gives the credit to the grid slot.
I fell for a version of it before running any code. I guessed the link was weak (0.37) and that the car explained little of it (8%). Both guesses were wrong in the same direction: I under-weighted the car.

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
Verdict: Confounded
Grid and finish are strongly linked, but car pace drives both: fast cars qualify near the front and race near the front. Compare drivers in the same car and grid’s effect shrinks by about 36%.
What’s left still isn’t proof that the grid slot itself causes better finishes. A driver who out-qualifies their team-mate may simply be quicker that weekend, and this model can’t tell the two apart.
What would change the verdict? A case where grid slots move for reasons unrelated to speed, such as grid penalties for engine changes. Comparing penalised drivers with their own unpenalised races would isolate the grid slot itself.

title: Starting at the front helps, but the car does much of the work
text:
Sources and caveats

Data: Jolpica F1 API, race results 2022–2025, pulled 14–15 Nov 2026. Licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the derived tables and this chart are shared under the same licence. n = 1,609 classified finishes from 1,838 results. Unofficial data; F1 names are trademarks of Formula One Licensing B.V., and this site isn’t affiliated with Formula 1.
Limitations:

216 results (11.8%) were dropped because the driver wasn’t classified. If front-runners retire at a different rate from back-markers, that tilts the result (survivorship bias). Some late retirements still count as classified.
The regression’s intervals are too narrow, because results within a race aren’t independent.
“Same car” means the same team in the same season; it can’t capture upgrades during a season or the difference between team-mates.
Positions are bounded at 1 and 20.

Synthetic? No.

title: About
text:
Seeing Things is a museum of patterns: a collection of short data stories that each ask a simple question, test it honestly, and give a verdict (causal, confounded, coincidence, reverse causation, or inconclusive).
Under every chart, the Looking Glass shows the exact SQL, Python and R that built it, so nothing has to be taken on trust.
It’s built by Abby Brazell, a data analyst in the Bay of Plenty, Aotearoa New Zealand, as a personal project using openly licensed public data. The code is on GitHub.

title: Seeing Things
text:
Most patterns are mostly noise. Here’s how to tell.
We’re brilliant at spotting patterns, and just as good at seeing things that aren’t there. Every exhibit in this museum pairs a real dataset with one clear picture, the statistical technique that tests it, and the brain trap that makes us misread it.
